title: Complex needs, independence and equitable access
blurb: Coordinate care for people with complex needs, promote independence, and make reasonable adjustments so everyone can access care.
question: Mrs Evans, who has a severe visual impairment, receives her outpatient letters in standard print and keeps missing appointments. What should the clinic do?

teach.body: People with complex needs often live with several long-term conditions, a disability, cognitive or communication difficulties, or social problems such as homelessness, all at once. Proficiency P7.5 asks nurses to respond to the challenges of providing safe, person-centred care for them; P7.9 to facilitate equitable access, advocate and make reasonable adjustments for people who are vulnerable or disabled. In plain English: same outcome, not same treatment. Some people need things done differently to get the same care.

teach.body: Some groups face barriers: people who are homeless, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities, people with learning disabilities or severe mental illness. Anyone in England can register with a GP surgery: you do not need ID, proof of address or proof of immigration status, and people without a permanent address can use a temporary address or the surgery's address (NHS website). Core20PLUS5 targets the most deprived 20% and locally identified PLUS groups. The public sector equality duty (s149) requires due regard to advancing equality of opportunity.

teach.caption: Proficiency P7.8: support people and families to maintain independence and avoid unnecessary interventions.

teach.body: Code 3.4 asks nurses to act as an advocate for the vulnerable, challenging poor practice and discriminatory attitudes. Under the Mental Capacity Act, a person is not treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success (s1(3)). So speak directly to the person, use their preferred communication method and aids, give information in an accessible format and allow time, rather than talking only to carers.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Jamie at the pre-assessment clinic
teach.body: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability and autism, epilepsy and asthma. Noise and waiting cause him distress. Nurse Ravi books the first appointment of the day with double time, sends an easy read letter, and records and flags Jamie's needs. He speaks directly to Jamie using pictures, involves his support worker as Jamie wishes, and coordinates one visit for bloods, ECG and a pharmacist review of his medicines, avoiding repeated trips.
teach.cite: Equality Act s20; AIS; Code 3.4; P7.5

teach.text: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty (Equality Act s20), not a favour. And the Accessible Information Standard covers needs from disability, impairment or sensory loss; a spoken language need on its own is met through professional interpreting instead.

items: s20 has three requirements: change a practice, deal with a physical feature, provide an auxiliary aid.
AIS: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs.
Anyone in England can register with a GP; no ID, proof of address or immigration status needed.
Enable independence; avoid doing for people what they can do with support.
Advocate: speak to the person directly and take all practicable steps to support their decisions.

summary: You can now make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010, apply the six stages of the Accessible Information Standard and help people from excluded groups access care. You can also coordinate care for people with complex needs while promoting independence and advocating for them.

A.q: A Deaf patient who uses British Sign Language is booked for a consent discussion. Which action meets the Equality Act duty to provide an auxiliary aid?
options: Ask her daughter, 14, to interpret
Write notes back and forth on paper
Book a qualified BSL interpreter
Speak slowly so she can lip-read
A.why: The third s20 requirement is to provide an auxiliary aid or service where a disabled person would otherwise be at a substantial disadvantage. A qualified BSL interpreter supports accurate information and valid consent (Equality Act 2010 s20; AIS).

whyNot.0: Using children to interpret is unacceptable except for immediate necessary treatment (NHS England interpreting guidance).
whyNot.1: Written English may not be accessible to a BSL user, especially for complex consent.
whyNot.3: Lip-reading is unreliable and may not be her preferred method.

A.q: Which list correctly gives the stages of the Accessible Information Standard?
options: Assess, plan, implement, evaluate, and review
Identify, record, flag, share, meet, review
Ask, advise, act, record, share, review
Screen, refer, treat, follow up, discharge
A.why: The AIS (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) has six stages: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review information and communication needs.

whyNot.0: This is the nursing process, not the AIS.
whyNot.2: Ask, advise, act is very brief advice on smoking.
whyNot.3: This describes a care pathway, not the AIS.

A.q: Dan, 45, is sleeping rough and wants to register with a GP but has no ID or proof of address. What should the nurse tell him?
options: He must first obtain photo ID
He can attend A&E but cannot register
He must be referred by a hostel before he can register
He can register with a temporary or surgery address
A.why: The NHS website says you do not need ID, proof of address or immigration status to register, and people without a permanent address can use a temporary address or the surgery's address.

whyNot.0: ID is not needed to register with a GP surgery.
whyNot.1: Everyone in England can register with a GP surgery.
whyNot.2: No referral is required to register.

B.q: Mr Clarke, recovering from a stroke, can wash his face and arms slowly with prompts. The ward is busy. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Encourage him to wash what he can, with help
Wash him fully to save time on a busy morning
Leave him to manage the wash without help
Ask his wife to come in and wash him
B.why: Nurses support people to maintain independence and avoid unnecessary interventions (P7.8). Doing for a person what they can do reduces function and dignity; rehabilitation depends on practice with support.

whyNot.1: Doing it for him undermines his recovery and independence.
whyNot.2: He needs prompts and help with parts he cannot manage safely.
whyNot.3: His wife may wish to help, but care should not be shifted to her for staff convenience.

B.q: Which of these needs falls within the scope of the Accessible Information Standard?
options: A patient who is Deaf and uses BSL
A patient whose first language is Polish
A patient who prefers emails to letters
A patient who works night shifts
B.why: The AIS covers information and communication needs relating to a disability, impairment or sensory loss, such as BSL use (NHS England DAPB1605).

whyNot.1: A spoken language need on its own is met through interpreting and translation, not the AIS.
whyNot.2: A preference unrelated to disability is outside the AIS.
whyNot.3: Working patterns are not a communication need under the AIS.

B.q: Leon is autistic and becomes very distressed in a noisy waiting room, so he often leaves before being seen. Which reasonable adjustment best addresses this?
options: Tell him the wait is the same for everyone
Offer the first appointment and a quiet space
Ask his mother to attend in his place next time
Discharge him for missed appointments
B.why: Changing a practice that puts a disabled person at substantial disadvantage is the first s20 requirement. A first appointment and quiet space reduces sensory overload so he can be seen (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7).

whyNot.0: Treating everyone the same ignores the legal duty to adjust.
whyNot.2: Leon is entitled to his own appointment; a parent attending instead removes his involvement.
whyNot.3: Discharging him for a disability-related barrier would be discriminatory.

C.q: Mr Patel, 81, has heart failure, diabetes and Parkinson's disease, takes 12 medicines and has fallen twice. What should the nurse request to address one key risk?
options: A falls prediction score
Bed rails for when he is in bed
A structured medication review
A referral for a wheelchair
C.why: NICE NG249 (2025) recommends considering a structured medication review to identify medicines that increase falls risk and adjust them. Polypharmacy is common in people with several long-term conditions (P7.5).

whyNot.0: NG249 advises against falls risk prediction tools.
whyNot.1: Bed rails are a restriction and do not address the causes of his falls.
whyNot.3: A wheelchair reduces mobility and independence rather than tackling the cause.

C.q: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability. On a ward round, the doctor discusses his treatment only with his support worker. What should the nurse do?
options: Let the support worker answer, as she knows him very well
Explain the plan to Jamie after the ward round
Ask the doctor to assess Jamie's capacity first
Use his communication passport; ask staff to speak to him
C.why: Nurses advocate for people who are vulnerable or disabled (Code 3.4; P7.9). All practicable steps must be taken to support Jamie's own decisions (MCA 2005 s1(3)), so staff should speak directly to him in his preferred way.

whyNot.0: Talking only to the support worker excludes Jamie from decisions about his care.
whyNot.1: Explaining afterwards does not involve him in the decision.
whyNot.2: Capacity is assumed; practicable steps to support him come before any assessment.

C.q: Mrs Evans has a severe visual impairment. Her clinic letters are in standard print and she has missed two appointments. What is the best response?
options: Phone her once and keep using standard letters
Ask her neighbour to read all her letters
Send large print and record and flag her need
Remove her from the list after two missed visits
C.why: Under the AIS, the service should identify, record, flag, share and meet her information need, providing an accessible format such as large print, and review it. s20(6) also makes accessible information a reasonable step.

whyNot.0: A single call does not meet her ongoing need for accessible information.
whyNot.1: Relying on a neighbour compromises her confidentiality and independence.
whyNot.3: Discharging her for a barrier the service caused would be discriminatory.

reteach.title: Ramps, not stairs
reteach.question: If a building has only stairs, is it fair to tell a wheelchair user that the stairs are the same for everyone?

blocks.body: Equitable access means removing the barriers that stop some people getting the same care: a ramp for a wheelchair, a BSL interpreter for a Deaf person, an early quiet appointment for someone overwhelmed by noise, a temporary address for someone homeless. The law (Equality Act s20) and the Accessible Information Standard make these adjustments duties, and good nursing makes them routine.

blocks.text: Treating everyone identically can be discrimination when it leaves a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage.

explain.body: Three requirements: change a provision, criterion or practice; deal with a physical feature; provide an auxiliary aid or service. Where information is involved, provide an accessible format.

test.q: Installing a hearing loop at a clinic reception is an example of which s20 requirement?
options: Providing an auxiliary aid or service
Changing a provision, criterion or practice
Meeting the public sector equality duty
Recording a communication need
test.why: A hearing loop is an auxiliary aid that prevents a disabled person being at a substantial disadvantage (Equality Act 2010 s20, third requirement).

whyNot.1: The first requirement changes how things are done, not equipment provided.
whyNot.2: The PSED (s149) is a broader duty of due regard, not a specific adjustment.
whyNot.3: Recording a need is an AIS stage, not an s20 requirement.

explain.body: Identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs arising from disability, impairment or sensory loss (DAPB1605, updated June 2025).

test.q: A nurse learns that a patient has aphasia after a stroke and needs picture-based information. Under the AIS, what should happen once the need is identified?
options: Tell the patient's family to explain things
Wait until the patient asks for help
Note it verbally at handover
Record and flag the need, then meet it
test.why: The AIS stages after identification are record, flag, share (with consent) and meet the need, then review it (NHS England DAPB1605).

whyNot.0: Relying on family does not meet the service's duty.
whyNot.1: Services must proactively meet identified needs.
whyNot.2: A verbal mention is not recording or flagging.

explain.body: Support people to do what they can for themselves, with prompts and aids, and avoid unnecessary interventions (P7.8).

test.q: Which approach best supports independence for a person relearning to dress after a hip fracture?
options: Dress her each morning to save her energy for therapy
Lay out clothes and assist where needed
Leave her to dress without any help
Keep her in nightwear until discharge
test.why: Enabling the person to do as much as possible, with assistance where needed, maintains function and dignity (P7.8).

whyNot.0: Dressing her removes the chance to relearn the skill.
whyNot.2: Leaving her without help risks falls and failure.
whyNot.3: Staying in nightwear reduces dignity and rehabilitation.

explain.body: Anyone in England can register with a GP without ID, proof of address or immigration status. People without a permanent address can use a temporary or the surgery's address.

test.q: An asylum seeker asks whether she needs proof of immigration status to register with a GP in England. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, a Home Office letter is needed
Yes, unless she pays privately
No, but she must show photo ID
No, it is not needed to register
test.why: The NHS website states you do not need ID, proof of address or proof of immigration status to register with a GP surgery.

whyNot.0: Immigration documents are not required for GP registration.
whyNot.1: Registration with an NHS GP is not linked to private payment.
whyNot.2: Photo ID is not required either.
